**What you will learn**

Distinguish the database, a private assignment and a released aggregate.

This chapter uses the public synthetic GiBleed practice connection from [Getting started](book-00-start.html).
**You need:** the packages and the matching practice connection described in
[Before you start](book-00-start.html#before-you-start).
Run the sections in order in one R session. All printed results below were computed
with dsOMOP and dsOMOPClient 2.10.5. They are teaching data, not clinical findings.

## Start this chapter

Start a fresh R session in the `book-work` directory created in
[Getting started](book-00-start.html#get-the-book-helpers). Run this setup first:


``` r
library(dsOMOPClient)
source("tools/book/display.R")
source("tools/book/connection.R")
source("tools/book/practice.R")
practice <- if (book_driver == "DSLite") book_practice("gibleed") else book_connect("gibleed")
conns <- practice$conns
names(conns)
```

```
#> [1] "site"
```

The `site` connection is ready. The shared `connection.R` selects DSLite or Opal and resolves the resource names.

## A shared table structure

OMOP is a common data model (CDM): a shared set of tables and column meanings.
`person` describes people; `visit_occurrence` describes visits; `observation`
holds observations and questionnaire answers; `death` records deaths. A *concept*
is a coded meaning, such as an education answer. A vocabulary supplies its name.

Ask which tables are available:


``` r
tables <- ds.omop.tables(conns = conns)
knitr::kable(tables$site)
```



|table_name            |schema_category |has_person_id |concept_prefix |
|:---------------------|:---------------|:-------------|:--------------|
|person                |CDM             |TRUE          |               |
|observation_period    |CDM             |TRUE          |               |
|visit_occurrence      |CDM             |TRUE          |visit          |
|visit_detail          |CDM             |TRUE          |visit_detail   |
|condition_occurrence  |CDM             |TRUE          |condition      |
|drug_exposure         |CDM             |TRUE          |drug           |
|procedure_occurrence  |CDM             |TRUE          |procedure      |
|device_exposure       |CDM             |TRUE          |device         |
|measurement           |CDM             |TRUE          |measurement    |
|observation           |CDM             |TRUE          |observation    |
|death                 |CDM             |TRUE          |               |
|note                  |CDM             |TRUE          |               |
|note_nlp              |CDM             |FALSE         |               |
|specimen              |CDM             |TRUE          |specimen       |
|fact_relationship     |CDM             |FALSE         |               |
|location              |CDM             |FALSE         |               |
|care_site             |CDM             |FALSE         |               |
|provider              |CDM             |FALSE         |               |
|payer_plan_period     |CDM             |TRUE          |               |
|cost                  |CDM             |FALSE         |               |
|drug_era              |CDM             |TRUE          |               |
|dose_era              |CDM             |TRUE          |               |
|condition_era         |CDM             |TRUE          |               |
|metadata              |CDM             |FALSE         |               |
|cdm_source            |CDM             |FALSE         |               |
|concept               |Vocabulary      |FALSE         |               |
|vocabulary            |Vocabulary      |FALSE         |               |
|domain                |Vocabulary      |FALSE         |               |
|concept_class         |Vocabulary      |FALSE         |               |
|concept_relationship  |Vocabulary      |FALSE         |               |

|concept_synonym       |Vocabulary      |FALSE         |               |

These are table names, not records. You can learn the structure without seeing a
person's dates or answers.

## Send a question to the data

DataSHIELD sends approved operations to the server. An *assignment* creates a
private object there. An *aggregate* returns a checked summary. The server can
refuse a result that lacks enough supporting people; a refusal is not a zero.

Ask for safe information about the person table:


``` r
ds.omop.table.stats("person", conns = conns)$per_site$site
```

```
#> $rows
#> [1] 2690
#> 
#> $persons
#> [1] 2690
```

The displayed `2690` is the lower end of a five-person band: from 2690
through 2694 people. This endpoint rounds down to a multiple of five in the
practice configuration; it has not told you the exact count. A later categorical
table may release exact supported cells through its own checks. Different
endpoints answer different questions and have different disclosure rules.

<div class="book-flow" role="img" aria-label="Your recipe goes to the server; private rows stay there; checked summaries return to you.">
<div><strong>You</strong>Choose events, variables and outputs.</div><span aria-hidden="true">→</span>
<div><strong>Server</strong>Compute with private records and apply release checks.</div><span aria-hidden="true">→</span>
<div><strong>You see</strong>Symbol names, schemas and checked summaries.</div>
</div>

## What stays on the server

You never download this book's assigned person table through DataSHIELD.
`person_id` becomes a pseudonym, but pseudonyms are still private row values.
Dates and ages are also private. Coarsening dates helps define a useful analysis;
it does not grant permission to fetch rows.

The practical sequence is: choose events, describe variables, assign a table,
then request an aggregate. Chapters 5–7 walk through it one small step at a time.

## Try it

Find the columns of the death table without asking for its rows.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>



``` r
knitr::kable(ds.omop.columns("death", conns = conns)$site)
```



|column_name             |cdm_datatype |db_datatype |concept_role      |semantic_class |fk_domain    |is_date |is_extension |is_untyped_identifier |is_sensitive |is_blocked |is_quasi_identifier |
|:-----------------------|:------------|:-----------|:-----------------|:--------------|:------------|:-------|:------------|:---------------------|:------------|:----------|:-------------------|

|death_date              |date         |text        |non_concept       |ordinary       |             |TRUE    |FALSE        |FALSE                 |FALSE        |FALSE      |TRUE                |
|death_datetime          |datetime     |text        |non_concept       |ordinary       |             |TRUE    |FALSE        |FALSE                 |FALSE        |FALSE      |TRUE                |
|death_type_concept_id   |integer      |real        |type_concept      |concept        |Type Concept |FALSE   |FALSE        |FALSE                 |FALSE        |FALSE      |FALSE               |
|cause_concept_id        |integer      |real        |attribute_concept |concept        |             |FALSE   |FALSE        |FALSE                 |FALSE        |FALSE      |FALSE               |
|cause_source_value      |varchar(50)  |text        |non_concept       |ordinary       |             |FALSE   |FALSE        |FALSE                 |TRUE         |TRUE       |FALSE               |
|cause_source_concept_id |integer      |real        |source_concept    |concept        |             |FALSE   |FALSE        |FALSE                 |TRUE         |TRUE       |FALSE               |

A schema describes fields, not people. A date field can exist in an empty table.

## Exercise 3: a pitfall to avoid

Ask for protected person-table statistics. Why is this different from a row download?

<details><summary>Solution 3</summary>


``` r
ds.omop.table.stats("person", conns = conns)$per_site$site
```

```
#> $rows
#> [1] 2690
#> 
#> $persons
#> [1] 2690
```

This returns the service’s protected summary; no person identifier is released.

</details>
## Recap

OMOP makes data structures familiar. DataSHIELD keeps patient rows at the server and checks released summaries.
